query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: The natural, thin passive iron oxide/hydroxide layer on pre-exposure Q235 steel acts as a protective barrier that suppresses corrosion in harsh environments at room temperature. At elevated temperatures, this film undergoes thermal destabilization—through enhanced solubility and micro-cracking—which compromises its integrity and leads to accelerated, localized corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel with its naturally formed oxide/hydroxide film from standard processing and storage, without any additional surface treatment.
generation.intervention: Characterize the as-received passive film on Q235 steel using surface techniques (e.g., XPS, SEM) and then expose well-characterized samples in controlled harsh environments (e.g., chloride-containing aqueous solution, possibly mildly acidic) at both room temperature (≈25 °C) and elevated temperature (≈70 °C). A set of samples should also have the passive film mechanically removed to serve as a control.
generation.conditions: Environment: A corrosion cell containing a saline solution with controlled pH and chloride concentration. Temperature: Comparison between room temperature (≈25 °C) and elevated temperature (≈70 °C). Duration: Exposure for a period sufficient to initiate noticeable corrosion effects (e.g., 7–14 days).
generation.structural_mediator: The intact passive iron oxide/hydroxide film on the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the intact passive film resists ingress of corrosive species (such as Cl⁻ ions and oxygen), thus inhibiting the electrochemical reactions that drive corrosion. At elevated temperatures, the film’s stability is compromised by thermal effects which induce dissolution, micro-cracking, or delamination, thereby exposing the underlying metal to accelerated corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated (bare or film-removed) Q235 steel, samples with the intact passive film will show significantly lower corrosion rates at room temperature, as evidenced by lower mass loss, higher impedance in EIS measurements, and less pitting. At elevated temperatures, the protective effect will diminish; the same samples will display higher corrosion rates—indicated by increased mass loss, more aggressive pitting, more negative corrosion potentials, and lower film integrity in surface analyses.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel in its natural, pre-exposure state (with its native oxide film) exposed to a controlled harsh environment at room temperature.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is valid for Q235 steel with its as-received passive film under controlled aqueous chloride (or acidic) environments. Variations in film composition due to processing, steel batch differences, or the presence of additional alloying elements could influence the observed behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise microstructure and chemistry of the native oxide layer may differ between samples and affect performance. Also, the threshold temperatures for film destabilization and the quantitative differences in corrosion rates under varied environments are not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Divide pre-exposure Q235 steel samples into two groups: one with the native passive film intact and one where the film is removed mechanically. Expose both groups to identical harsh corrosive environments at room temperature (≈25 °C) and elevated temperature (≈70 °C). Monitor the surface film integrity using XPS/SEM along with measuring corrosion rates via mass loss, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and potentiodynamic polarization tests.
measurements: Mass loss over a fixed exposure period
Surface film integrity and morphology (via XPS and SEM)
Electrochemical parameters (corrosion potential, current density, impedance spectra)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no statistically significant difference in corrosion resistance between samples with and without the native passive film at room temperature, or if elevated temperature does not lead to a measurable degradation in the film accompanied by accelerated corrosion (i.e., similar corrosion rates across temperature conditions), then the hypothesis is rejected.
